title: Fragmented ETH: Prethermalization, Timescales, and Ensemble Inequivalence
authors: C. L. Sriram, Soumya Kanti Pal, Lea F. Santos
abstract: We investigate how finite quantum systems with strong long-range interactions approach thermal equilibrium. Nearly conserved quantities inherited from the fully connected limit fragment the Hilbert space and give rise to a many-body spectrum split into energy bands. As a result, equilibration becomes anomalously slow and proceeds through long-lived prethermal plateaus. This two-stage equilibration process is, however, not universal. We uncover the mechanism that determines which observables and initial states exhibit, or evade, prethermal plateaus. We also develop a perturbative theory that provides analytical expressions for both the height of the prethermal plateau and its timescale. Despite the lack of global ergodicity, quantum chaos develops within individual energy bands, enabling the definition of microcanonical ensembles within the bands. This supports a band-resolved formulation of thermalization, which we term fragmented eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (fETH). Unlike conventional ETH, finite-size scaling in fETH obeys a symmetry-imposed selection rule that restricts which system sizes can be compared. This band-resolved description has direct consequences for equilibrium statistical mechanics. While microcanonical ensembles remain confined to a single band, canonical ensembles mix different bands. This mismatch explains ensemble inequivalence without invoking equilibrium phase transitions. Our results apply to a broad class of Hamiltonians exhibiting Hilbert-space fragmentation.
summary: This paper analyzes how quantum systems with long-range interactions approach equilibrium by developing the fragmented ETH (fETH). It shows that Hilbert space fragmentation causes slow prethermalization and predicts ensemble inequivalence because different statistical ensembles sample different parts of the energy spectrum. The work provides analytical tools to quantify these non-equilibrium dynamics.
main_problem: The paper investigates how finite quantum systems with strong long-range interactions approach thermal equilibrium when global ergodicity is lost due to Hilbert space fragmentation.
main_result: It proposes the fragmented ETH (fETH) as a band-resolved description of thermalization, identifying that ensemble inequivalence arises because microcanonical ensembles are confined to single energy bands while canonical ensembles sample across multiple bands.
method: The authors develop a perturbative theory to analytically predict prethermal plateau heights and timescales, alongside developing a symmetry-constrained finite-size scaling framework for fETH.
model_or_system: The study focuses on finite quantum systems with super long-range interactions (e.g., the spin-1/2 transverse-field Ising chain). The Hamiltonian exhibits fragmentation due to nearly conserved quantities inherited from the fully connected limit.
key_observables: Prethermal plateau height and timescale, survival probability ($P_S(t)$), microcanonical vs. canonical ensemble predictions.
important_parameters: The interaction decay exponent $\alpha$ (super-long-range regime $\alpha < d$), system size $N$, and the ratio of coupling strengths to local fields.
main_assumptions: The hybridization between neighboring energy bands is assumed to be weak enough ($\alpha < d$) for the band structure approximation to hold; conventional ETH fails due to fragmentation.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically maps out spectrum fragmentation, quantum chaos within bands, prethermal timescales, conditions governing prethermalization, and the symmetry-imposed selection rule for fETH.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the physical problem (fragmentation due to long-range interactions), then proposing fETH as the necessary modification to ETH, deriving analytical tools (perturbative theory), and finally demonstrating the consequences of this fragmentation on equilibrium statistical mechanics via ensemble inequivalence.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium dynamics in complex many-body systems, providing a refined theoretical framework (fETH) for understanding thermalization when standard assumptions of ergodicity break down due to system structure or interactions.
